text:
# First Chapter

Likewise, in the *Noble Jewel-Heap Scripture* <term>Ratnakūṭasūtra</term> <gloss>a collection of early Mahāyāna scriptures</gloss> <margin>Tibetan translation 16b; See the same text cited below at chapter 17, verse 33</margin>: At that time, those five hundred monks <term>bhikṣu</term> <gloss>ordained Buddhist monks</gloss> <margin>The Tibetan version adds that they were "attainers of meditation" <note>original: dhyāna lābhin</note>, compare the Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā 38. 8</margin> did not enter into, did not penetrate, and did not find conviction in the Lord's teaching of the Dharma. They rose from their seats and departed. Then the Lord <note>at 그 time</note> created two illusory monks <term>nirmitaka</term> <gloss>artificially manifested beings</gloss> <margin>Reconstructed from the Tibetan and the citation at 17. 33; for this term see the Perfection of Wisdom <note>original: Prajñāpāramitā</note> 442. 14</margin> on the path by which those monks were traveling.

Then those five hundred monks approached the path where those two created monks were. Having approached, they said: "Where are you venerable ones going?" The two created ones replied: "We are going to the forest dwellings. There we will abide in the dwellings of the blissful touch of meditation <term>dhyāna</term> <gloss>states of deep mental absorption</gloss> <margin>folio 12b; for the phrase "abides in blissful touch" <note>original: sukhasparśaṃ viharati</note>, see Mahāvyutpatti 245. 649, 255. 3. 5 and Śikṣāsamuccaya 200. 18, where Bendall notes Lalitavistara 357. 12 and Mahāvastu volume I, 623</margin>. For we do not enter into, nor penetrate, nor find conviction in the Dharma that the Lord teaches; we stand aloof and are struck with terror." 

Then those five hundred monks said: "Venerable ones, we too do not enter into, nor penetrate, nor find conviction in the Lord's teaching of the Dharma. We stand aloof, we are terrified, and we fall into terror. Therefore, we shall abide in the forest dwellings in the dwellings of the blissful touch of meditation." 

The two created ones replied: "In that case, venerable ones, let us reach an agreement and not dispute. For non-dispute <term>avivāda</term> <gloss>absence of contention</gloss> <margin>Compare Śikṣāsamuccaya 263. 18: "that which does not dispute follows the dharma of a monk" (see also 195. 7, 281. 14); Mahāvyutpatti 245. 1189; Lotus Sūtra 14. 33: "I am to utter an infallible word; refrain from disputing about it: the science of the Tathāgata is beyond reasoning." In the manuscript for the Lotus, "dispute" <note>original: vivāda</note> is replaced by "despair" <note>original: viṣāda</note>. Non-dispute is defined in the Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha 15. 11 as "the acceptance of what is spoken by the teacher" <note>original: gurūktasyāṅgīkaraṇa</note>. For the six roots of dispute, see Majjhima Nikāya volume II, page 245. All the world disputes, except for the monks, see same work page 120.</margin> is the highest of a monk's <term>śramaṇa</term> <gloss>ascetic seeker</gloss> qualities. <unclear>******</unclear> <margin>Compare below, folio 100a. Our text here is abbreviated.</margin> For the sake of abandoning what, venerable ones, have you set out?" They replied: "We have set out for the sake of abandoning passion, hatred, and delusion."

<summary>This page recounts a narrative from the Ratnakūṭasūtra where the Buddha creates two illusory monks to counsel five hundred followers who are terrified by his profound teachings. The illusory monks encourage the group to focus on meditation and the practice of non-dispute as a way to overcome their spiritual crisis.</summary>
<keywords>Ratnakūṭasūtra, bhikṣu, dhyāna, nirmitaka, avivāda, non-dispute, meditation, Buddhist monks, śramaṇa, passion, hatred, delusion</keywords>
